# FDG9149

> CONSIDER adding Span- or Memory-based alternatives to methods that accept arrays or strings.

Framework Design Guidelines, 3rd edition, section 9.12 Operating on Buffers.

## How it is checked

- Check: sdk (partial coverage)
- Diagnostics: CA1844
- Automatic fix: no
- Severity: library suggestion, application none, test none
- Status: verified

Library only: the reason given is a greater number of callers, and an application changes its own callers (as for FDG9021). CA1844 reports a class derived from Stream that overrides the array-based ReadAsync or WriteAsync without overriding the Memory-based one (probe with SDK 10.0.402: reported when targeting net10.0, not net472, whose Stream has no Memory-based overloads; a Stream that overrides only Read and Write is not reported). That is one case of a missing Memory-based alternative; other methods that accept arrays or strings are not seen, and whether a string or array parameter is a buffer is what it means, so coverage is partial. CA1844 has no code fix; adding an override or an overload changes no existing signature. Span<T> and Memory<T> types need .NET Core 2.1 or later, or the System.Memory package on .NET Framework and .NET Standard 2.0 (see FDG9137).

## From the book

The Span and Memory types support arrays, but also support additional kinds of buffers—such as `ReadOnlyMemory<char>` and `ReadOnlySpan<char>`, which can represent a portion of a `System.String` value. Providing Span- or Memory-based alternatives allows for a greater number of callers to the functionality you’re offering.

Generally, your users will expect you to provide the alternatives as method overloads on the same type as the array- or string-accepting method.

```csharp
// Previously:
public void AppendData(byte[] data, int offset, int count) {
  if (data == null)
    throw new ArgumentNullException(nameof(data));
  // bounds argument validation here

  // implementation
}

// With a ReadOnlySpan<byte> overload:
public void AppendData(byte[] data, int offset, int count) {
  if (data == null)
    throw new ArgumentNullException(nameof(data));
  // bounds argument validation here so parameter names are correct

  AppendData(data.AsSpan(offset, count));
}

public void AppendData(ReadOnlySpan<byte> data) {
  // implementation, from previous version
}
```

For static methods, it can make sense to have the array- or string-accepting methods on a high-level type, and to create a new low-level type for working with Span or Memory (section 2.2.4).
